title: Cardioselective beta-blockers for reversible airway disease
authors: Salpeter S, Ormiston T, Salpeter E
followUp: single dose, or continued treatment for 3 to 28 days
population: Patients with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with reversible obstruction, documented by methacholine challenge, a rise in forced expiratory volume in one second of at least 15% after a beta2-agonist, or asthma as defined by the American Thoracic Society
funder: Internal sources: Santa Clara Valley Medical Center, USA. External sources: No sources of support supplied.
result: Issue 4, 2002, of this Cochrane review: 19 trials of a single dose and 10 of continued treatment, all randomised, blinded and placebo-controlled. A single dose of a cardioselective beta-blocker reduced the forced expiratory volume in one second by 7.46% (95% CI 5.59 to 9.32), while the response to a beta2-agonist given afterwards rose by 4.63% (2.47 to 6.78) against placebo. Treatment lasting 3 to 28 days produced no change in that volume (-0.42% of baseline, 95% CI -3.74 to 2.91), in symptoms or in inhaler use, and a beta2-agonist response of 8.74% (1.96 to 15.52) persisted. In the subgroup with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease the treatment effect on that volume was -5.28% (-10.03 to -0.54) for single doses and 1.07% (-3.30 to 5.44) for continued treatment. The full text in PubMed Central carries the same effect estimates after a search to June 2011 that added no eligible study, and reports 240 patients in the single-dose trials and 141 in the continued-treatment trials, a risk difference for respiratory symptoms of 0.01 (-0.02 to 0.03) and 0.01 (-0.02 to 0.04) respectively, and cardioselectivity of at least 20-fold for beta1 over beta2 receptors.
